reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Michael got to school with his red bag. He was a little shy at the door. His teacher smiled and said good morning.

It was dress-up time. Michael wanted to be a fireman. He found a big black coat. He found shiny red boots. He pushed his feet into the boots first. Then he tried to push socks on top. The socks slid off. He fell over on the rug and laughed. He pulled the boots off. He put the socks on first. Then the boots went on. They stayed on. He stood up tall.

At lunch, Michael ate his apple and bread. He could smell the soup in his cup. After lunch, the class lay on mats for a rest. Michael did not sleep. He watched his friend Lily draw a cat on the computer with the teacher.

At home time, Michael put on his coat. He pointed at his socks. "Socks first," he said to his mom. "Then boots." His mom laughed. Michael marched out the door like a fireman. "Nee naw," he called. "Nee naw."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Lincoln stood alone in the nursery. His new baby sister was in the crib. She was very small. She made a little crying sound.

Lincoln wanted to help. Babies like crackers, he thought. So he went to fetch his cracker from the table. He held it out to her. "Cracker?" he asked. The baby kept crying. She turned her small face away.

Mom came in. "She is hungry," Mom said. Mom picked up a bottle. It was warm from the warm water. Mom held the bottle for the baby. The baby drank the milk. Her crying stopped. Her eyes went soft and sleepy.

Lincoln watched. Then he knew. His sister did not eat crackers yet. She drank milk. So Lincoln went to get his toy bunny. He set it by the crib, close to her. "For when you are big," he said. The baby made a small happy sound.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Charlie stood at the basketball court with a big bag of beanbags. She wanted to throw them all by herself. She threw one, two, three into the hoop. A boy named Sam waited and waited.

"More beanbags," said Charlie. She held the bag tight like a magnet on the fridge. Sam's face went sad. His shoulders drooped low.

Then Charlie looked at Sam. She looked at the long line of beanbags. She handed one to Sam. "Your turn," she said. Sam threw it and the beanbag went in. He jumped up and down. "Your turn now," said Sam.

So they took turns. One person throws. Then the next person throws. Charlie threw a beanbag, and then Sam threw a beanbag. They counted together. One, two, three, four, five.

Then Daddy rolled a big ball to Charlie. She patted the ball with both hands and caught it. She laughed. She rolled it back to Sam so he could try.

Sam caught the ball too. He gave Charlie a pat on the back. "Good catching," he said. "Again tomorrow?" asked Charlie. Sam smiled and picked up the last beanbag.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Lincoln ran to the school garden. Today he would plant carrot seeds. His teacher, Ms. Rosa, gave him a small shovel. Lincoln dug little holes in the dirt. He dropped the seeds in, one by one. "Grow, grow, grow!" he said.

Every day Lincoln watered the dirt. Then one morning, green leaves popped up. Lincoln clapped his hands. But wait. Little green leaves grew everywhere, even between his carrots. What a puzzle! "Those must be weeds," said Lincoln. "Weeds grow where I don't want them." He pulled some out. Then he saw a tiny leaf right where a carrot should be. Was it a weed too? He did not want to hurt his carrot.

"Ms. Rosa, is this a weed?" Lincoln asked. Ms. Rosa knelt down. "Look at the rows," she said. "Your carrots grow in a line. That leaf is in your line." Lincoln smiled big. It was a baby carrot! He patted the dirt around it. "You get to stay," Lincoln told the leaf. Behind him, a line of little green tops waved in the wind.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Nora was at Grandma's house. Lunch was ready. Grandma had made crunchy toast with jam. Nora ran to the table.

"Wash hands first," said Grandma. "We count to twenty." Nora held her hands under the water. She wanted toast now, not later. She started to march back to the table.

"Nora, we scrub with soap for twenty seconds," said Grandma. "Let's count together." They put soap on their hands. "One, two, three." They rubbed and rubbed. The bubbles grew big and white. Nora watched the bubbles cover her fingers. "Ten, eleven, twelve." The clock's little hand moved a tiny bit. "Nineteen, twenty!"

"Done!" said Nora. Grandma gave her the answer to her tummy's growl. Warm toast, sweet jam. Nora took a big bite.

"After lunch, we wash again," said Grandma. Nora nodded. She held up her soapy hands and said, "One, two, three!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Emmett was in the kitchen with Grandma. Grandma wanted to make a berry smoothie. Emmett wanted to help.

"First, wash the berries," said Grandma. Emmett touched the berries. They were cold and bumpy. He smelled them. "They smell sweet!" he said. He tasted one little berry. "Yum. Sweet and sour."

Then Grandma plugged in the blender. Mom always plugged it in, not Emmett. Grandma said, "Ready? Here we go."

The blender made a big, loud noise. Brrrrr! It was very loud. "Too loud!" shouted Emmett. He put his hands over his ears. Press, press.

The loud sound got smaller. It was quiet now. Emmett peeked at the blender. Then he took one hand off his ear. The noise got big again. He put his hand back. Small again. One hand off, one hand on. "Grandma, my hands make it quiet!" he said.

"Yes, ears under hands, quiet ears," laughed Grandma. She stopped the blender. "One, two, three scoops of smoothie," she said. Emmett counted too. "One, two, three!"

Emmett looked at the pink cup. He heard the last little buzz die away. He smelled the berries again. He touched the cold cup. He tasted the smoothie. "Best loud machine ever," he said.

Grandma laughed. "After our snack, we can sweep the floor. The berries made a wild mess." Emmett looked down. Berries everywhere. He got the little broom.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Riley was at Grandma's house. She wanted to find the room with the big toy box. Grandma had five rooms upstairs, but which one?

Grandma said, "The toy box hides behind door five. You will know it when you see it!"

Riley looked at the first door. It had a big 1 on it. She looked at the next one. It had a big 2. Then a 3. Then a 4.

At the last door, Riley stopped. It had a big 5. She held up her hand. "One, two, three, four, five," she counted, wiggling her fingers. Five fingers. And a 5 on the door!

She pushed the door open. Inside was the toy box, and a soft blanket on top. Grandma had made the blanket quiet and cozy. "You found it!" Grandma laughed from the hall.

Riley hugged the blanket. "Five fingers, five door," she said. Then she counted ten toys, one by one, all the way to ten, and lined them up on the bed.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Leah loved the beach. She played in the sand all morning. She made a crunchy sand cake with shells on top. The sea was big and splashy. Leah could not swim yet, and she wished she could.

That afternoon, Mom took her to the local pool. A kind teacher named Rosa waited in the water. "Today we will float on our backs," Rosa said. Leah looked at the water. It was deep. She held the pool wall tight.

"What if I sink?" Leah asked. Rosa smiled and held out her arms. "I will hold you while you float," she said. Leah lay back into the water. Rosa's hands held her back, warm and steady. Leah did not sink. She floated, looking up at the big blue sky. "I'm floating!" she called. Rosa laughed softly. "Yes, you are." Then Leah kicked her feet, and they moved together across the pool, all the way to the steps. "Again," said Leah, holding out her arms.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Hazel wanted her animal book. She could not find it anywhere. She looked in the toy box. She found a ball. She found a red truck. No book.

Then Hazel had a big idea. "I will make a library," she said. She set her toys in a straight line on the bench. Trucks went with trucks. Animals went with animals. She put her stuffed bear with the lion. The bear made a soft sound when she squeezed him.

Next she sorted her play food. Apples went with bananas. The pretend peas went with the pretend corn. "These are for eating," she said. "But not really eating."

At last she found the book shelf box. The animal books were all together in one spot. There was her book, with a tiger on the cover. Hazel sat down by the bear and the lion. She read them the tiger page, twice.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
story:
The lights went out. The whole house turned dark. Jules stood still in the hall. He could not see his own feet.

"Mom, the lamps stopped!" he called. Mom came with slow, careful steps. She held baby Anna on her hip. "The power is out," Mom said. "We need our flashlight." Dad patted the shelf by the door. He patted the table, too. No flashlight there.

Jules thought hard. He asked, "Where is it hiding?" Then he knew the answer. "The kitchen drawer!" he said. He took Mom's hand. They went together, step by step. The drawer slid open with a soft sound. Inside was a long, hard shape. It was cold and smooth. "I found it!" said Jules.

Mom clicked the button. The flashlight lit up. A round spot of light planted itself on the wall. Jules gasped. The lamps were still dark. The house was still dark. But the flashlight shone anyway! "It works with no power," Jules said. Mom smiled. "That is true."

The light made a circle on the floor. Jules moved his hand in front of it. His hand made a bunny shape with long ears. Anna laughed and kicked her feet. Mom made a dog shape next. Jules laughed too.

They sat on the rug together. The flashlight glowed warm and steady. Dad found some bread and apple slices. They had a picnic right there in the dark. The lights stayed off all night. That was fine. The little light was enough. "Bunny is sleepy," Jules whispered. He made the bunny lie down on the rug.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Victor wanted to build a house for his toy bird. He picked a square block. He put it on the floor for the wall. Then he found a triangle for the roof. "The roof can fly up high," said Victor, and he placed it on top.

His friend Mia came in. She pointed at a block on the rug. "That is a new shape," she said. The square was turned. One corner pointed up. Victor looked at it. He turned it back down. "Look," he said. "It is the same square." Mia clapped. "A square is a square!"

They made the house together. Victor put a rectangle at the door. Mia set a circle by the window. The bird sat on top. Victor gave the bird a kiss on its head. "Next we need a bed," said Mia. She handed him one more little square.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story: Aiden found a book at school. It had a dog on the front. He wanted to read it to his friend Mia. Aiden sat down and opened the book. He put his finger at the right side of the page. He tried to say the words. They came out all mixed up. Mia looked upset. "That is not the story," she said. Miss Polly came over. She did not say much. She took Aiden's hand and put his finger at the left side of the page. Aiden slid his finger across, left to right. This time the words came out smooth. "See the dog run," he read. Mia smiled and clapped. Aiden lifted the page and turned it. "Next page," he said. "I have an idea. We read all the way to the back." They read together, page by page, until the dog found his bone.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Natalie ran into the nursery. A new baby was here! He was her baby brother, Sam.

Sam lay in his flat little bed. Natalie wanted him to smile. She made a funny face. Sam did not smile. Then Sam began to cry. Loud cries! Big tears!

"He is not talking," Natalie said. Then she had an idea. Babies cannot talk yet. Maybe the cry was his way of asking! "Does he need milk?" she asked. Mommy said, "Let's try." Mommy gave Sam a bottle. Sam drank and drank. The crying stopped. Sam made a small, soft sound. Then he closed his eyes and went to sleep.

Natalie tiptoed out. She got her paper and glue. She made a card. She drew a road on it, so Sam could follow it home to her. Mommy taped the card on the wall by the flat little bed. "For Sam," said Natalie. "When he wakes up."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Austin sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. He saw a poster of an ear. He heard a baby cry in the next room. He touched the squishy seat with his hand.

The nurse gave Austin a sticker and a strawberry. Austin sniffed it with his nose. It smelled so sweet. He took a bite. Yum! It tasted sweet too.

Then his mother held his nose for a silly game. "Hold still," she said. Austin bit the strawberry again. It tasted plain, like nothing much. He made a funny face.

The nurse laughed. Austin let go of his nose. He took another bite. Sweet again! He saw that his nose made the taste strong.

Austin got down from the chair. He put the sticker on his shirt. "More strawberry," he said.

The nurse opened a little fridge. Inside was one more strawberry, big and red. What a surprise!

At home, Austin yawned. His mother said, "Time to sleep soon." Austin held his strawberry in his hand. He sniffed it one more time with his nose. Sweet dreams smelled like strawberries.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Hunter had a big red drum. He wanted to bang it loud. He lifted the sticks up high. BANG! BANG! BANG!

Dad came running. "The baby is sleeping," Dad whispered. "She needs quiet now."

Hunter looked down the hall. The baby was small in her crib. She rubbed her eyes. A bird outside the window flew away fast.

Hunter wanted to play slow and soft. He tapped the drum. Tap. Tap. Tap. That was quiet. The baby stayed asleep.

"Can I do one loud bang?" Hunter asked.

"One," said Dad.

Hunter raised the sticks. He made his loudest BANG. The baby woke up and cried loud too.

"Oops," said Hunter. He tapped quiet again. Tap. Tap.

The baby blinked. Then she yawned. Then she went back to sleep.

Dad patted Hunter's head. "My quiet drum man," he said.

Hunter grinned and tapped his toes instead.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Madelyn wanted to build a house for her toy sheep. She found a block with three sides. "That is a triangle," she said. She found a block like a door. "That is a rectangle." She found a round ball. "That is a circle." Then she found a flat cracker-shaped block. Was it a square? She was not sure.

She cut a piece of string. She laid it along one side. Then she laid it along the next side. The string fit just the same. She laid it on the third side, and then the fourth. The string still fit just the same. All four sides matched.

"A square!" said Madelyn. She set it on top for a roof. But the roof looked weak and wobbled. She turned the square block so it sat flat. Now it did not wobble at all. The sheep went inside. "Good night, sheep," said Madelyn.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story: Raphael was at school. He was painting a big star. It was yellow. Then his friend Ben grabbed the brush. Ben painted right over the star. Raphael felt angry. His face got hot. He pushed the paint cup away and sat in the corner. He did not say anything. His teacher, Miss Ana, came over. She sat down next to him. "Raphael, can you tell me what is wrong?" she asked. Raphael looked at his shoes. "Why should I tell her?" he thought. Then he said, "I feel sad. My star is all gone." Miss Ana nodded. "Let's look," she said. The yellow star was still there. It was hiding under the blue paint. Miss Ana got a clean brush. Raphael painted the star again, even brighter. It looked real. He felt happy now. "My star is back!" he said. Ben said, "I like it." Raphael smiled. "Want to paint with me?" he asked. Ben said, "Yes!" So they painted side by side.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Everett sat at the dinner table. The soup was hot. Mama said, "Blow on it." Everett blew with his mouth. Then he touched the bowl with one finger. "Warm now," he said. His fingers felt the smooth bowl.

He heard a slurp. Papa was slurping his soup. Everett laughed. His ears liked that sound. Then he smelled something sweet. His nose went up, up, up. "Cookies!" he said. His eyes looked for them. But the kitchen was dark. It was hard to see. "Where are the cookies?" he asked.

"I will turn on the light," said Papa. Click. The light went on. Now Everett could see. There they were, on a rough wooden plate. Everett took a small bite. "Yum," he said. His tongue tasted cinnamon. It tasted like summer. Mama tapped her spoon. Ding! Everett tapped back. Ding, ding!

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Lennon sat at the snack table. Her jar of applesauce had a tight lid. She pulled and pulled. The lid did not move.

"Try asking for help," said her friend Milo.

How could words open a jar? Lennon wondered. She decided to try.

"Can you help me, please?" she asked Miss Rosa.

Miss Rosa smiled. "Of course." She turned the lid. Pop! It came off.

"Thank you," said Lennon.

Miss Rosa said, "You said the magic words. Those words help big people know you need them."

Later, Milo spilled his cup. Milk ran across the table. He looked at his shoes.

"Sorry," said Milo.

"It's okay," said Miss Rosa. She wiped the table with a cloth.

At play time, Lennon saw her spotted phone toy under the shelf. It was too far for her hand. Could words work again?

"Can you help me, please?" she asked.

Miss Rosa reached down. She got the phone out.

Lennon held the phone up high. "It worked again!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Cooper sat in the middle of the back seat. Mommy drove the car. Cooper wanted his water cup. It was on the floor. "Help, please, Mommy," he said. Mommy reached back at the red light. She gave him the cup. "Thank you," said Cooper. Mommy said, "You're welcome." Cooper blinked. That was a new thing to say!

He drank some water. Then the car went bump. Water splashed on his shirt. "Sorry," said Cooper. "That is okay," said Mommy. The car was quiet. Cooper counted cars out loud. "One car. Two cars. Three cars."

Then Cooper laughed. He had an idea. "Mommy, what do I say after thank you?" he asked. Mommy smiled. "You say you're welcome," she said. Cooper practiced. "Thank you, cup. You're welcome, Cooper." Mommy laughed too. The car drove on, nice and warm.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Gabriella put on her little apron. Today she would bake muffins for her family. The community kitchen smelled like warm bread and old apples. Her grandma helped her mix the batter. Gabriella stirred slowly. She watched the flour hide inside the wet mix.

"Who will tell us when the muffins are done?" Gabriella asked. Grandma pointed to a round timer. "We can ask that little friend," she said. Grandma turned the dial, and it made a tick, tick, tick sound. Then the muffins went into the big oven. Grandma slid the tray in herself, because ovens are very hot.

While they waited, the family played a game at the long table. Gabriella matched red cards and blue cards. She laughed when Papa made a silly face. Soon the game got very busy. Everyone forgot to watch the clock.

Then the timer rang out loud. Beep, beep, beep! "The muffins!" said Gabriella. She clapped her hands. Grandma put on her big mitts and took out the tray. The muffins were golden and warm. Gabriella gave one to Mama, one to Papa, and one to Grandma. She bit into her own muffin. "The little friend told us," she said, "and we did not burn them."

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Rowan wanted to help make sandwiches. Mama gave him bread, cheese, and a spoon. "Can I cut the bread?" he asked. "I will use the knife with you," said Mama. Her hand held his hand.

First Rowan looked for a corner to start cutting. The bread was a square. It had four corners. He put the knife on one corner. Then Mama gave him a round cracker. "Cut this one," she said. Rowan looked for a corner. He looked and looked. There was no corner anywhere. A circle is round and has no corners. "No corner!" said Rowan. "No corner," said Mama. She smiled.

Rowan cut the square bread into two triangles. He cut the cheese into a long rectangle. Then he made a face on his plate. The crackers were circles for eyes. The water cup tipped and the water did not spill, because the cup was round and it rolled back. Rowan sang a little song. Mama closed the bread bag. Then Rowan took a big bite of his sandwich face. "Yum!" he said. "Yum!" said Mama.

story: Cooper ran fast into the playroom. His big red ball was gone! He looked under the small chair. He looked in the toy box. No ball. Then he heard a funny sound. Flap, flap. It came from the closet. The closet door was open. Cooper peeked in. The cold air tickled his bare toe. "Ball!" he said. The big red ball sat inside, next to Daddy's shoe. Cooper pulled the door wider and grabbed it. The door swung shut with a soft click. Now it was closed. Cooper pushed it. Open. He pulled it. Closed. Open, closed, open, closed. He laughed. It was like a game. Then he pushed it shut and held it there. He sniffed the air. He could smell soup. Daddy was cooking in the kitchen. Cooper ran to see, slow at the door, then fast across the floor. "Daddy, my ball was hiding," he said. Daddy stirred the pot and smiled. Cooper stood back, far from the sharp edge of the counter, and watched the steam rise.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Isla stood in the bathroom with Mama. It was time to wash her face. But Isla did not want water in her eyes. "I will close my eyes," she said. "Then the water can't get me." She covered her eyes with her hands.

Splash! Mama washed her face with warm water. Isla could not see the towel. She could not see Mama. She could hear the water drip, drip, drip. She could smell the soap. Her tummy felt a little funny. "Mama?" she called.

"I am here," said Mama. Isla opened her eyes. She saw Mama smiling. She saw the soft blue towel. She touched the towel. It was warm and fluffy. "Water went splash," said Isla. "My eyes were closed. I could not see!" She giggled. Mama dried her hands and made the sink all tidy. "Now we can buy a little towel just for you," said Mama. Isla hugged the blue towel tight.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Jasmine sat at the big table. She had paper and crayons. She wanted to draw a picture for a party. Mom was making a cake for the party, and Jasmine was hungry for cake.

First she drew the sun. She picked the yellow crayon. Round and round went the sun. Yellow sun on white paper.

Next she drew the grass. She picked the green crayon. Green grass, soft and long. She patted the paper with her hand, soft like grass.

Now she wanted the sky. She picked the gray crayon. She held it up. Then she looked out the window. The sun was shining. The sky was not gray at all. The sky was blue. Jasmine put the gray crayon down.

She picked the blue crayon. Slowly, slowly, she made the sky. Blue sky over the green grass. Blue sky by the yellow sun.

Mom came over. "What a pretty day," said Mom.

Jasmine held up her paper. "Look, Mom! Blue sky!" She marched around the table, holding her picture high.

"Let's hang it up for the party," said Mom.

Jasmine smiled at her picture. Yellow sun, green grass, blue sky. She clapped her hands. "Party day!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Colton stood in the big restaurant kitchen. The cook, Rosa, had made warm toast. She put a small knife with butter in front of him. "Can I try?" Colton asked. "Yes, you can," said Rosa. Colton held the knife. He spread the butter. The butter made the toast shiny.

Next came the milk. Colton lifted the little jug. He poured slowly. Too fast! Milk splashed onto the table. A small puddle sat there, white and shiny like snow. Colton frowned. "What now?" he asked. Rosa pointed to a blue cloth with a turtle on it. Colton took the cloth. He wiped the puddle. The table was dry again.

Colton picked up the jug once more. This time he tipped it just a little. The milk went into the cup. Not one drop fell. Colton smiled and took a big drink of milk.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
story:
The lights went out at the farmhouse. Everything went dark. "Wow!" said Kai. He wanted his teddy bear.

Kai ran to the kitchen. Bump! He hit a chair. "Ouch," said Kai. Dad came fast. "In the dark, we walk slowly," said Dad. "Hold my hand."

Kai held Dad's big hand. They took one slow step. Then another step. No bumps! They found the flashlight. Dad clicked it on. "A light!" said Kai. "So pretty!"

Mom lit the fireplace. The room turned warm and orange. "Let's have a dark party," said Mom. They sat on the rug. They ate crackers. Kai hugged his teddy bear.

Then the lights came back on. The whole house glowed. "Yay!" said Kai. He clapped his hands. "More dark party tomorrow?"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Julia looked out the window. The sky was gray. Then rain began to fall. Drip, drip, drip. Julia saw big puddles on the path. She wanted to jump in them. "I will wear my boots," she said.

Julia pulled on her red rain boots. One boot, two boots. She put on her yellow rain coat. It had a triangle pocket. Julia held Mama's hand. They went outside.

The rain went pitter patter. Julia found a puddle. She stepped in it. The water went splash. Julia looked at her socks through the boot tops. They were dry! Her feet were warm and dry. "Dry feet, dry feet," she sang.

Then the wind blew. It blew Julia's hat right off. The hat flew down the path. Julia waited. She watched it land in the grass. Then she walked over slowly and picked it up. She put it back on her head.

The rain stopped. The sun came out. It was sunny now. Mama said, "Look up." Julia saw a rainbow in the sky. It had red, and yellow, and blue. Julia held her hat on her head and smiled. "Hello, rainbow!" she said.

story:

At last Sam held the book out. "Your turn," Sam said.

Felix took the book. Miss Jo sat down next to him. "Read it to me," said Felix. Miss Jo read the words on the page. The dog ran to the salty sea. The dog got wet. Felix laughed.

Daddy read the same page. The dog ran to the salty sea again. The dog got wet again. Felix clapped his hands.

"Same words!" said Felix. "Miss Jo said the sea. You said the sea too."

Daddy turned the page, and there was the dog, shaking water everywhere. Felix laughed so hard he fell over on the rug.

story:
Connor sat at the dinner table. He had chicken on his plate. He also had peas and milk. Then he saw something stuck to his sleeve.

It was a little feather. Soft and white. "Look, Mom!" said Connor. "A feather!"

"Where did that come from?" Mom asked.

Connor thought hard. He thought about his toy box. His monkey had soft fur, but no feathers. His ball had no feathers. His teddy had no feathers either. Then he thought about the backyard. A bird had been there this morning. The bird was pecking near the fence.

"The bird!" said Connor. "The bird has feathers. One fell on me!"

Mom laughed. "A bird feather on a chicken night," she said. "That is a funny dinner surprise."

Connor put the feather in his pocket. "Maybe the bird wants it back," he said. "Can we leave it on the fence after dinner?"

Mom smiled. "Yes," she said. "But first, eat your peas."

Connor ate one pea. Then two. Then all of them. The feather waited in his pocket, ready for the fence.

story:
Jordan stacked the soft blocks at daycare. He made a tall tower. It was a good tower.

His friend Mia ran over. "Come to my house!" she said. "We can play in my snow fort."

Jordan wanted to go now. He ran to Teacher Ana. "I go to Mia's house now!" he said.

Teacher Ana shook her head. "Not today, Jordan. It is sleepy time first. Tomorrow is the day after today. You sleep tonight, and then it is tomorrow."

Jordan looked out the window. The winter sun was bright. But sleep came after the sun went away. He would have to wait.

Jordan ate his snack. He played with trucks. He wondered, "Is it tomorrow yet?" Teacher Ana laughed. "Not yet. Now is still today."

After nap, Jordan's daddy came. "Can it be tomorrow now?" Jordan asked. "Not yet," said Daddy. "First we eat dinner. Then you sleep. When you wake up, it is tomorrow."

Jordan ate his dinner. He put on his soft pajamas. He closed his eyes.

Then he opened them again. The sun was up! "Is it tomorrow?" he asked. Daddy smiled and nodded. Jordan ran to find his shoes. "Mia's house!" he shouted. "Today is the day!"

story:
Henry went to the park today. Yesterday it rained, so the sandbox was wet. Now the sun was out, and the sand was just right for digging. Henry wanted to dig a big, big hole. He started to dig. He dug and dug. "Look, Dad! My hole is getting deep!" Dad smiled and sat on the bench. "I will wait here," said Dad. Henry found a smooth white stone in the sand. It was his treasure. He put it in his sweater pocket. He wondered where his hole would go when he went home. Would it still be there later? Would it be there tomorrow?

At bedtime, Henry asked Dad, "Where did today go?" Dad said, "After you sleep tonight, today will be called yesterday." Henry thought about that. His hole was at the park right now. But tomorrow, his digging day would be yesterday. He hugged his stone and closed his eyes.

In the morning, Henry ran to the window. The sun was up. "It is today now!" he said. "And my digging is yesterday!" At the park, his hole was still there. But the rain had filled it with water. Two ducks were swimming in it. Henry laughed. "My hole is a pond now!"

story:
Stella found a big red book at daycare. It had a bear on the front. The bear held a blue umbrella.

"I want to know who drew the bear," Stella said.

She opened the book. First she looked at the very front. There were little marks there. "Those marks are words," said her friend Tom. "Words tell us things."

Miss Ana came over. "Do you see the names?" she asked. "One name is for the person who wrote the words. One name is for the person who drew the pictures."

"Who draws the pictures?" asked Stella.

"That person is called the illustrator," said Miss Ana. She pointed. "Here is the illustrator's name. Liz Park drew this bear."

Stella smiled. She put her finger on the name. Then she turned the first page. Then the next page. The pages went front to back. The bear found his umbrella at the end!

"I can draw a bear too," said Stella. She marched to the art table. It was a noisy room, full of kids. She picked up a pencil.

She drew a bear with a red hat.

"Look, Tom!" she said. "I am the illustrator."

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
story:
The lights went out. The whole house went dark. Jules stood on the grass in the backyard. "I can't see anything!" he said. "How will I find my ball?"

Dad came out with a big blanket. "We can wait out here," said Dad. "One, two, three, we count the dark away."

Jules squinted. "Is that a bush? No, that's the swing." He blinked. Then he blinked again. The swing came out of the dark, slow and soft. He could see it now.

"One, two, three," he counted. "I see the swing! I see the sandbox! I see my toy fish in the sand!"

"That fish is not real," laughed Dad. "Real fish swim. That fish naps in dirt."

Jules tiptoed over. He picked up the fish. His eyes could see the door now too. "Dad, look! The dark got softer!"

Just then the porch light blinked back on. The whole backyard lit up like morning. Jules held up his fish. "Hello again, house," he said. "Hello again, grass."

Aubrey woke up early at Grandma's house. She reached for her bunny. Bunny was not there. "Oh no," said Aubrey. "Bunny is lost."

Aubrey held Grandma's hand. They walked to the big box by the door. Aubrey peeked in. There was a hat. There was a mitten. There was a shoe. And way at the bottom, there were two soft ears. "Bunny!" cried Aubrey. She pulled him out and gave him a big hug.

story:
Victoria was at the beach with her family. The wind blew her hat right off. Daddy caught it and laughed.

Next to the beach was a little pool. Victoria's big sister Maya swam in the deep end. Maya went under the water and came up smiling. Victoria wanted to go there too.

"Wait, wait, wait," said the swim teacher, Miss Jo. "You start here." Miss Jo pointed to the shallow end. Victoria stood there. The water came up to her tummy only. She blew bubbles. She kicked her legs. She tried again. Then she tried again.

Victoria looked at the deep end. Maya stood there, and the water went up to Maya's shoulders. Victoria looked at her own water, up to her tummy. The pool was small at one end and big at the other.

Victoria picked up a wet leaf from the pool edge. It felt slimy. She gave it to Daddy, and he did not let it break.

"Watch me!" Maya called from the deep end. Victoria watched. Then she practiced her kicks some more. Kick, kick, kick. Miss Jo held her hand.

"Tomorrow we try more," said Miss Jo. Victoria nodded. The wind blew softly on the water. "See you tomorrow, deep end," Victoria said.

story:
Mohamed sat at the kitchen table. He had big paper and red paint. He wanted to paint a flower for his mom.

Mom put out the brushes. "Put on your old shirt," she said. Mohamed shook his head. He sat down fast. He dipped his brush in the red paint.

He painted one petal. Then another petal. A big drop fell. It fell right on his shirt. His clean white shirt now had a red spot. "Oh no," said Mohamed.

Mom brought him an old blue shirt. Mohamed pulled it on over his own shirt. He painted more petals. Drips fell on the blue shirt. His own shirt stayed clean. No more red spots.

He painted the flower all red. Then he made a stem. Mom helped him sort the brushes in a cup. Mohamed held up his paper. The flower was big and bright.

Mom smiled. "Now let's wash that little red spot," she said. Mohamed looked at his blue shirt. It had ten spots. He laughed. "The old shirt caught them all," he said.
